plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 6: Applications of Newton's Laws
plan.contextChunk: This figure combines a pictorial diagram with two force diagrams drawn beside it. At the left, a pulley hangs on a short stem from a beige ceiling beam; its gray grooved wheel carries a yellow cord whose two ends drop vertically to a pair of wood-grain square blocks, the higher one at the left labeled m1 and the lower one at the right labeled m2. To the right, under the headings "Block 1" and "Block 2", each block is redrawn alone as the same wood-grain square with a red vector T pointing straight up from its top edge and a red weight vector pointing straight down, labeled w1 and w2 respectively. The two tension arrows are drawn the same length, while the downward arrow on block 2 is noticeably longer than the one on block 1. Keeping the tension arrows identical while letting the weight arrows differ is the comparison the reader is meant to make. The figure sets up the Atwood machine, in which two unequal masses joined over a frictionless pulley share one string tension and accelerate equally in opposite directions.

interactionPlan.concept: In an Atwood machine two masses joined by one cord over a frictionless pulley share a single string tension, so it is the difference in their weights — not the tension — that produces a common acceleration, equal in magnitude and opposite in direction for the two blocks.
elements: Beige ceiling beam across the top left with two small mounting bolts
Short gray vertical stem/axle connecting beam to pulley
Gray grooved pulley wheel with concentric rings and hub
Yellow cord passing over the pulley groove, two vertical segments hanging down
Left wood-grain square block labeled m1, hanging higher
Right wood-grain square block labeled m2, hanging lower
Heading text 'Block 1' above the left free-body diagram
Heading text 'Block 2' above the right free-body diagram
Free-body block 1: wood-grain square labeled m1 with red upward vector labeled T from its top edge and red downward vector labeled w1 from its bottom edge
Free-body block 2: wood-grain square labeled m2 with red upward vector labeled T (same length as block 1's T) and a longer red downward vector labeled w2
Vertical dashed reference line / ground level marks to gauge how far each block has moved
Optional acceleration arrows (a) beside each block: downward on the heavier block, upward on the lighter
Legend keying red = force vectors, and note that the two T arrows are deliberately drawn identical

interactions.teaches: That the two tension arrows stay identical no matter how the masses differ, while the weight arrows and the resulting acceleration grow with the mass difference — zero difference means zero acceleration even though tension is still nonzero.
interactions.label: m₂ (kg), with m₁ fixed at 2.0 kg

interactions.teaches: That once released, the connected blocks move with equal-magnitude, opposite-direction accelerations: the heavier block descends exactly as far as the lighter one rises, because one inextensible cord ties their motions together.
interactions.label: Release sequence

demo_steps.title: Equal masses: balanced
demo_steps.narration: With m₂ set equal to m₁, the two weight arrows are the same length and the system hangs still. Both tension arrows are drawn identical — and each one exactly cancels its block's weight.

demo_steps.title: Make m₂ heavier
demo_steps.narration: Increase m₂ and watch only the w₂ arrow lengthen; the two T arrows stay the same length because one cord carries one tension. Block 2's downward arrow now outweighs its tension while block 1's tension outweighs its weight.

demo_steps.title: Release
demo_steps.narration: Let go: the unbalanced force on each block sets the system moving. Acceleration arrows appear — downward on m₂, upward on m₁, with identical length.

demo_steps.title: Equal and opposite motion
demo_steps.narration: As the cord runs over the pulley, m₂ descends exactly as far as m₁ rises. Their accelerations are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, a = (m₂ − m₁)g / (m₁ + m₂).

demo_steps.title: Push the difference further
demo_steps.narration: Increase m₂ toward 8 kg: the weights diverge more, the acceleration arrows grow toward g, and the blocks separate faster — yet the single tension shared by both blocks remains one common value.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: One cord means one tension acting equally on both blocks — so the acceleration comes entirely from the difference of the weights, and the two blocks must accelerate by the same amount in opposite directions.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Left half: pictorial Atwood machine — a beige horizontal ceiling beam at top with two bolt heads, a short gray stem down to a gray concentric-ring pulley wheel, a thin yellow cord over the groove with two vertical strands dropping to two wood-grain (tan, wavy-grain) squares with gray outlines; the left block sits higher and is labeled m₁ to its left, the right block sits lower and is labeled m₂ to its right. Right half: two separated free-body diagrams under bold headings 'Block 1' and 'Block 2', each a copy of the wood-grain square with its mass label at the left. From the top edge of each block a red arrow labeled T points straight up; both T arrows must always be drawn the same length. From the bottom edge a red arrow labeled w₁ or w₂ points straight down, with w₂ visibly longer than w₁ by the mass ratio. When released, add slimmer arrows labeled a beside each free-body block (down for the heavier, up for the lighter, equal lengths) and let the pictorial blocks translate vertically by equal opposite amounts with a faint dashed horizontal line marking each block's starting height. Keep all force vectors red on a white background; labels in italic serif math style.
interactionPlan.figureNotes: The comparison the reader should make is tension arrows identical vs. weight arrows unequal.

authoredContext:
Atwood Machine A classic problem in physics, similar to the one we just solved, is that of the Atwood machine, which consists of a rope running over a pulley, with two objects of different mass attached. It is particularly useful in understanding the connection between force and motion. In the figure, m1=2.00kg and m2=4.00kg. Consider the pulley to be frictionless. (a) If m2 is released, what will its acceleration be? (b) What is the tension in the string?

T=2m1m2m1+m2g (This is found by substituting the equation for acceleration in the figure(a), into the equation for tension in the figure(b).)

An Atwood machine and free-body diagrams for each of the two blocks.

An Atwood machine consists of masses suspended on either side of a pulley by a string passing over the pulley. In the figure, mass m sub 1 is on the left and mass m sub 2 is on the right. The free body diagram of block one shows mass one with force vector T pointing vertically up and force vector w sub one pointing vertically down. The free body diagram of block two shows mass two with force vector T pointing vertically up and force vector w sub two pointing vertically down.

Strategy We draw a free-body diagram for each mass separately, as shown in the figure. Then we analyze each diagram to find the required unknowns. This may involve the solution of simultaneous equations. It is also important to note the similarity with the previous example. As block 2 accelerates with acceleration a2 in the downward direction, block 1 accelerates upward with acceleration a1. Thus, a=a1=−a2.

discrepancies: Free-body vector labels (T, w₁, w₂) are drawn in red in the generated figure, whereas the source uses black bold labels with overbar arrows next to red arrows — a small but visible color/style deviation.
A legend ('force vectors' / 'acceleration' with an italic footnote) is added at the bottom of the diagram; the source has no legend, and its 9–10 px italic text is uncomfortably small at inline size.
Blue acceleration arrows and dashed 'start' reference lines do not exist in the source; they are hidden in the default 'held' phase but the legend advertising them is visible by default.

Arrow-length proportions differ somewhat from the source: in the source Block 2's tension arrow is drawn noticeably longer and w₂ extends much further below, while the generated T arrows are comparatively short relative to the weights (physically correct, but visually less similar).
Composition is left-heavy: the pictorial and both FBDs sit in the upper two-thirds with a large empty band below, unlike the tighter source crop.
evaluation.notes: Structurally faithful reproduction of the Atwood machine plus both free-body diagrams with correct physics (T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁+m₂), a = (m₂−m₁)g/(m₁+m₂)) and a rich, genuinely useful set of interactions; main weaknesses are red instead of black vector labels, an added tiny-text legend/acceleration overlay absent from the source, and loose bottom whitespace.
action_items: Render the T, w₁, w₂ vector labels in black bold serif with overbar arrows (as in the source) so the default state matches the static figure; reserve color only for the arrows themselves.
Remove or shrink-and-relocate the bottom legend and italic footnote (or show it only once acceleration arrows become visible) to avoid unsourced clutter and 9 px unreadable text.
Tighten the layout: reduce the empty band below the figure and enlarge the pictorial/FBD group so labels read comfortably at inline size.
Fix the UI panel label wrapping ('m₂ = 4.0 kg (m₁ fixed at 2.0 kg)' currently wraps across three lines) so the slider caption reads as one line.

feedback.rationale: The concept, physics, and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are implementation details like label color/style, legend clutter, whitespace, and text wrapping.

discrepancies: Held phase shows T = 26.1 N with w₂ = 39.2 N while the blocks are drawn stationary — for a genuinely 'held' system the net force on each block should be zero (or an external hold force shown), so the labelled state is internally inconsistent for unequal masses.

Blue acceleration arrows and dashed 'start' reference lines are added to the free-body diagrams in the released phases; these do not appear in the source figure (default state is clean, so impact is limited).

Pictorial details differ slightly: the source ceiling beam runs off the left edge of the frame and the pulley bracket/axle assembly is larger and more detailed; the generated beam is a short floating plank.
In the source pictorial the m₂ block is drawn slightly larger than m₁ (visually cueing the mass difference); the generated blocks are identical in size regardless of the mass slider.
